note.happening: Tesla fell 1.18% to 380.14. note.business: Several numbers point to the business itself getting weaker. Sales in the latest quarter changed -0.17% from a year earlier, after 15.78% growth two quarters ago. Operating margin (the profit kept from each sales dollar before interest and tax) fell to 3.35% from 4.74%. Free cash flow (cash left after running the business and paying for investment) dropped to 3.3B over the last 12 months, from 6.8B. Inventory is up 15% while quarterly sales are up 0%. Unsold cars can force price cuts, which would put margins under more pressure. Each dollar invested now earns 5¢ a year, against 33¢ three years ago. Those are changes to demand, margins and cash. note.worth: The methods disagree badly, and the gap comes down to growth. A discounted cash flow (DCF) model values a company from the cash it is expected to produce. Today's price-to-sales of 14.5 sits at the 73rd percentile of its 5-year range, and the trailing price-to-earnings ratio is 418.3. If operating margin falls to 2%, the DCF value is 27.91. My range uses the lower half of Tesla's own valuation history, because the cash-flow models cannot reach today's price under any growth they test.
